lessons.title: Understanding the budget
lessons.html:
What a budget is

A budget is a financial plan for a period, usually a year, broken into months. It shows the expected income and the money each section may spend. For a supervisor of a stable yard, stud or farm section, the budget is your spending limit and your target.

Typical expense lines for an equine unit

CategoryExamples
FeedHay, concentrates, supplements
BeddingShavings, straw
Veterinary and medicinesVaccines, dewormers, call-outs
FarrierTrims, shoeing
LabourWages, overtime, protective clothing
Repairs and maintenanceFences, stables, water systems
Fuel and transportBakkie, horsebox, tractor
Capital itemsNew saddles, a horsebox (usually a separate capital budget)

How the budget is built

Budgets are usually based on last year's actual spending, adjusted for planned changes (more horses, a new arena) and price increases such as inflation and feed price rises. You may be asked to give input: number of horses, feed per horse per day, farrier cycles and planned projects. Accurate input leads to a realistic budget.

Fixed and variable costs

  • Fixed costs stay the same regardless of activity, such as insurance or a fixed salary.
  • Variable costs change with activity, such as feed and bedding per horse.

Knowing which is which helps you explain why spending goes up or down.

Your responsibilities

  • Know your budget lines and limits.
  • Spend only on approved items, within your authority level.
  • Follow the procurement policy: quotes, orders and approvals.
  • Keep records and report variances.

lessons.title: Controlling spending and reporting variances
lessons.html:
Controlling expenditure

  1. Plan purchases: use the monthly budget figure, not the annual total, as your guide. Seasonal items like winter hay may be planned for specific months.
  2. Get quotes: follow the company rule, for example three quotes for items above a set amount in ZAR.
  3. Use purchase orders: an approved order before buying, so that spending is authorised.
  4. Check deliveries: count and check quality against the order and delivery note before signing.
  5. Match invoices: order, delivery note and invoice must agree before payment.
  6. Control stock: keep feed and medicine stock records to prevent waste and theft.

Monitoring: budget versus actual

Each month, compare what you spent with the budget.

LineBudget (R)Actual (R)Variance (R)
Feed45 00049 500-4 500 (over)
Bedding8 0007 200+800 (under)
Farrier12 00012 0000

A variance is the difference between budget and actual. Investigate significant variances: why did feed cost R4 500 more? Perhaps the hay price rose after drought, or two extra horses arrived, or feed was wasted.

Taking action

  • For overspending: find savings elsewhere, reduce waste, renegotiate prices, or ask management for approval of extra spending with reasons.
  • For underspending: check that it is a true saving and not a delayed purchase or a skipped task like maintenance.
  • Report variances in writing, with causes and proposed actions, by the deadline.

Integrity

Never split orders to avoid approval limits, accept gifts from suppliers that could influence you, or buy for personal use with company funds. Report any irregularities.

Key points

  • A budget is a plan and a spending limit for each line.
  • Know fixed and variable costs.
  • Use quotes, purchase orders and invoice matching.
  • Compare budget with actual monthly and investigate variances.
  • Report variances with causes and actions; act with integrity.
